slides.heading: Welcome: Sexual Harassment Prevention
bullets: What sexual harassment is and the two main types
Harassment from coworkers, supervisors and families
Texting, social media and your role as a bystander
How to report, and why retaliation is prohibited
slides.narration: Hi, and welcome to Sexual Harassment Prevention training at Spectrum Squad. Whether you are a brand new R B T, an experienced B C B A, or part of our office team, this course is for you. Everyone deserves to feel safe and respected, wherever our work takes us. Over the next ten minutes or so, you will learn what sexual harassment looks like, including the two main types. We will talk about other kinds of harassment, about texting and social media, and about what to do when you see something happen to someone else. Most importantly, you will learn exactly how to report a concern and why you never have to fear payback for speaking up. Let's get started.

slides.heading: What Sexual Harassment Is
bullets: Unwelcome conduct that is sexual or based on sex
Words, jokes, gestures, images, touching or messages
Can happen between people of any gender
Against the law and against Spectrum Squad's policy
slides.narration: Let's start with the basics. Sexual harassment is unwelcome conduct that is sexual in nature, or that targets someone because of their sex. That includes harassment based on pregnancy, sexual orientation, or gender identity. It can be spoken comments, jokes, gestures, pictures, touching, or messages on your phone. The key word is unwelcome. It does not matter whether the person meant it as a joke. What matters is the effect on the person receiving it. Harassment can happen between people of any gender, including people of the same gender. It is against federal law, it is against Nevada law, and it is against Spectrum Squad's policy. There are two main types, and we will look at each one next.

slides.heading: Type One: Quid Pro Quo
bullets: Means "this for that"
A job benefit or decision tied to sexual favors
Usually involves someone with power over your job
Even one incident should be reported right away
slides.narration: The first type is called quid pro quo. That is a Latin phrase that means this for that. It happens when someone with power over your job makes a work decision depend on sexual favors, or on putting up with sexual advances. Picture this. A lead technician who helps build the schedule tells a new R B T, if you go out with me this weekend, I will make sure you get the full caseload you asked for. That is quid pro quo. The offer does not have to be spelled out, and the person does not have to follow through on it. Even one incident like this is serious and should be reported right away.

slides.heading: Type Two: Hostile Work Environment
bullets: Unwelcome conduct that is severe or pervasive
Makes work intimidating, hostile or offensive
Can build up from repeated "small" comments
Speak up early; don't wait until it's unbearable
slides.narration: The second type is a hostile work environment. This happens when unwelcome sexual or sex based behavior is severe, or happens often enough, that it makes work feel intimidating, hostile, or offensive. One very serious act, like unwanted touching, can be enough on its own. Other times it builds up over weeks. Think about a clinic break room where a coworker keeps making comments about a teammate's body, shows sexual memes on his phone, and laughs it all off as just joking around. Each comment might seem small, but together they create a place where people dread coming to work. Spectrum Squad's policy asks you to speak up early, long before behavior ever reaches the level of breaking the law.

slides.heading: Harassment Beyond Sex
bullets: Race, color, religion and national origin
Disability, genetic information and age
Sexual orientation and gender identity or expression
Same standards and same reporting steps apply
slides.narration: Harassment is not only about sex. Federal and Nevada law also protect people from harassment because of race, color, religion, national origin, disability, genetic information, and age for workers forty and older. Nevada law also specifically protects sexual orientation and gender identity or expression. So mocking a coworker's accent, making jokes about a teammate's religious head covering, or calling someone old and slow are all forms of harassment. Imitating a person's disability is harassment too, and in a field built on supporting people with disabilities, that should never happen here. Everything you learn in this course about sexual harassment applies to these other forms as well. The same standards of conduct apply, and the same reporting steps apply.

slides.heading: From Coworkers and Supervisors
bullets: Peers, leads, BCBAs, office staff or owners
Unwanted touching, comments on looks, date pressure
Close supervision must always stay professional
Once someone says no, that answer is final
slides.narration: Harassment can come from anyone at work. That includes fellow technicians, office staff, B C B As, managers, and even the owner. Here are a few examples from our field. A B C B A who supervises your sessions keeps standing very close, rubs your shoulders while giving feedback, and asks about your dating life. A coworker you carpool with between school sessions asks you out again and again after you have already said no. Supervision in our work is close and often one on one, and that closeness should always stay professional. Asking a coworker out one time is not harassment by itself. But once a person says no, that answer should be respected. Pressure after a no is a problem.

slides.heading: In Clients' Homes and the Community
bullets: Parents, relatives, visitors or school staff can harass
You don't have to tolerate it to keep a case
If you feel unsafe, end the session and leave safely
Report it to your supervisor the same day
slides.narration: A lot of our work happens in clients' homes, and that brings a special risk. Harassment can come from a client's parent, a relative, a roommate, a visitor, or staff at a school. Here is a realistic example. During a home session, a client's uncle keeps commenting on your body, asks for your personal number, and one day stands in the hallway so you cannot easily get past him. That is harassment, even though he does not work for Spectrum Squad. You do not have to put up with it to keep a case. If you ever feel unsafe, it is okay to end the session safely, leave, and call your supervisor. Then report what happened that same day. Spectrum Squad can change the plan, such as reassigning the case, so you are protected and the child still gets care. If a client shows sexual behavior as part of their diagnosis, that is handled clinically with your B C B A, but you should still tell your supervisor.

slides.heading: Texting and Social Media
bullets: Rules apply to texts, DMs, posts and shared photos
Off-hours messages can still be workplace harassment
Keep messages with families and staff professional
Don't delete it: screenshot, save and report
slides.narration: Harassment does not stop when you leave a session. It can happen through texts, direct messages, social media comments, or shared photos. A coworker who sends flirty messages late at night after you have asked them to stop, or a parent who follows you online and keeps commenting on your pictures, can create a hostile environment even if it all happens after hours. Keep your own messages with coworkers and families professional, and use the communication tools that Spectrum Squad's policy approves. If you receive something inappropriate, do not delete it. Take screenshots, note the date and time, and save them. Then report it.

slides.heading: Bystanders Can Make a Difference
bullets: Step in or redirect the conversation
Check in privately with the person targeted
Report what you saw, even if you weren't the target
You don't need to be sure it's illegal to report
slides.narration: What if you see harassment happen to someone else? Let's say you are at the clinic and you hear a coworker making crude comments to a new technician who looks uncomfortable. You could step in by changing the subject, asking the new technician to come help you with something, or simply saying, that's not okay. Later, check in with them privately and let them know you noticed. You can also report what you saw, even though you were not the target. You do not need to be sure it counts as illegal harassment before you report. Your job is just to share what you saw. HR and leadership will look into it from there.

slides.heading: How to Report a Concern
bullets: Tell your supervisor, HR or the owner
If it's your supervisor, go straight to HR or the owner
Report in person, by phone, by email or in writing
Share what, who, when, where and any witnesses
slides.narration: If you experience harassment or see it happen, please report it. You can go to your supervisor, to HR, or to the owner of Spectrum Squad. You do not have to follow a strict chain of command. If the person harassing you is your own supervisor, skip them and go directly to HR or the owner. You can report in person, by phone, by email, or in writing. Try to share what happened, who was involved, when and where it happened, and whether anyone else saw it. Bring any screenshots or notes you saved. It is always better to report early, because a small problem is much easier to fix than a big one. Spectrum Squad's policy lists the specific people to contact.

slides.heading: No Retaliation and Fair Investigations
bullets: No punishment for reporting in good faith
Protects reporters, witnesses and people who help
Concerns are looked into promptly and fairly
Info shared only with those who need to know
slides.narration: Spectrum Squad strictly prohibits retaliation, and so does the law. Retaliation means treating someone worse because they reported harassment, supported someone else's report, or took part in an investigation. Examples would be cutting a technician's hours after she complains, suddenly giving her the hardest cases and the longest drives, threatening her, or encouraging coworkers to freeze her out. This protection applies when you report in good faith, which means you honestly believe what you are reporting, even if the investigation cannot confirm it. If you think you are facing retaliation, report it the same way you would report harassment. So what happens after a report? Spectrum Squad will look into it promptly and fairly. That usually means talking with the people involved and any witnesses. Everyone gets a chance to share their side. Information is kept as private as possible and shared only with people who need to know. Total secrecy cannot be promised, because others may need to be interviewed to find the truth. If policy was broken, Spectrum Squad will take action, which can include discipline up to and including termination.

slides.heading: Supervisor Duties and Outside Help
bullets: Supervisors must report harassment they learn about
Be supportive, but never promise to keep it secret
You may contact the EEOC
Or the Nevada Equal Rights Commission
slides.narration: If you supervise anyone, including B C B As who oversee technicians, you have an extra responsibility. When you see harassment, or someone tells you about it, you must report it to HR or the owner right away, even if the person asks you to keep it quiet. Be kind and supportive, but do not promise to keep it secret, and do not try to investigate it on your own. Everyone should also know that outside agencies exist. You have the right to contact the federal Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, called the E E O C, or the Nevada Equal Rights Commission. These agencies enforce the laws against workplace harassment and discrimination. There are time limits for filing with them, so if you are thinking about it, reach out sooner rather than later. Contacting them is also protected from retaliation.

slides.heading: Recap and Quiz
bullets: Harassment can come from anyone, anywhere you work
Report to your supervisor, HR or the owner
Retaliation is never allowed
Now take the quiz: you need 80% to pass
slides.narration: Let's recap. Sexual harassment includes quid pro quo, where job benefits are tied to sexual favors, and hostile work environment, where unwelcome conduct makes work intimidating or offensive. Harassment based on race, religion, disability, age, and other protected traits is not allowed either. It can come from coworkers, supervisors, clients' family members, or visitors, and it can happen in person or through texts and social media. If you see it, you can step in and report it. Report to your supervisor, HR, or the owner, and if your supervisor is the problem, go around them. Retaliation is prohibited, investigations are fair and kept as private as possible, and outside agencies are there too. Thank you for helping keep Spectrum Squad safe and respectful. Now it is time to take the quiz. You need a score of eighty percent to pass. Good luck!

quiz.question: A lead technician tells a new RBT she will get the extra hours she asked for if she goes on a date with him. What is this?
choices: A normal scheduling conversation
Quid pro quo sexual harassment
Not harassment, because no hours were actually changed
Only a problem if it happens more than once
quiz.explanation: Tying a job benefit to a date or sexual favor is quid pro quo harassment. The offer does not have to be carried out, and one incident is enough to report.

quiz.question: During a home session, a client's uncle keeps commenting on your body, asks for your number and blocks the hallway when you try to leave. What should you do?
choices: Ignore it, because he is not a Spectrum Squad employee
Put up with it so the family stays happy with the case
Quietly stop showing up to that home without telling anyone
End the session safely if you feel unsafe and report it to your supervisor that day
quiz.explanation: Harassment from family members and visitors counts. Your safety comes first, and reporting the same day lets Spectrum Squad change the plan to protect you.

quiz.question: The BCBA who supervises you keeps making sexual comments about your appearance. Where should you report it?
choices: Directly to HR or the owner
Only to that BCBA, to follow the chain of command
Nowhere until your next performance review
In a post on social media so others know
quiz.explanation: When the harasser is your supervisor, skip them and go straight to HR or the owner.

quiz.question: A coworker keeps sending you flirty texts late at night after you asked them to stop. What is the best step?
choices: Delete the texts so you don't have to see them
Do nothing, because it is after hours on a personal phone
Screenshot and save the messages with dates and times, then report them
Reply with jokes to keep things friendly
quiz.explanation: Off-hours messages can still be workplace harassment. Saving screenshots preserves evidence for your report.

quiz.question: In the clinic break room, you hear a coworker making crude comments to a new technician who looks uncomfortable. What is the best bystander response?
choices: Stay out of it, since you are not the target
Redirect or step in, check in privately with the technician, and report what you saw
Tell the new technician to toughen up
Report it only if you are certain it is illegal
quiz.explanation: Bystanders can interrupt, support the person targeted and report. You do not need to be sure it is illegal before reporting.

quiz.question: Right after an RBT reports harassment, her hours are cut and she is given the longest drives. What is the best way to view this?
choices: It may be retaliation, and she should report it the same way she reported the harassment
It is normal scheduling and nothing can be done
It is allowed if her original complaint could not be confirmed
It only counts as retaliation if someone puts it in writing
quiz.explanation: Treating someone worse for a good-faith report is retaliation, which is prohibited even if the investigation cannot confirm the original complaint.

quiz.question: A coworker regularly mocks a teammate's accent and makes jokes about her religious head covering. Which statement is true?
choices: It is fine because it is not sexual
It only matters if the teammate complains in tears
It is acceptable friendly teasing between coworkers
It is harassment based on protected traits, and the same reporting steps apply
quiz.explanation: National origin and religion are protected traits. Harassment based on them follows the same standards and reporting steps as sexual harassment.

quiz.question: An RBT tells her clinical supervisor about harassment by a parent but asks him to keep it secret. What should the supervisor do?
choices: Promise to keep it secret and take no action
Confront the parent and investigate it on his own
Be supportive, explain he cannot keep it secret, and report it to HR or the owner right away
Wait to see whether it happens again
quiz.explanation: Supervisors have an extra duty to report harassment they learn about right away, and they should not promise secrecy or investigate on their own.

quiz.question: You are interviewed as a witness in a harassment investigation. How is confidentiality handled?
choices: Information is kept as private as possible and shared only with those who need to know, but total secrecy can't be promised
The details are shared with the whole team so everyone learns
The accused person is never told about the complaint
Witnesses are free to discuss it with coworkers afterward
quiz.explanation: Investigations are kept as private as possible, but others may need to be interviewed, so complete secrecy cannot be promised.

quiz.question: Besides reporting inside Spectrum Squad, which outside agencies can an employee contact about workplace harassment?
choices: The Nevada DMV and the Better Business Bureau
Only the agency that certifies behavior analysts
Only the local police department
The EEOC and the Nevada Equal Rights Commission
quiz.explanation: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and the Nevada Equal Rights Commission enforce laws against workplace harassment, and contacting them is protected from retaliation.
